abstract: Dr. Calvert presents a systematic approach to evaluating pelvic pain using eight key history questions. Through multiple case examples, he illustrates the differential diagnosis of chronic and acute pelvic pain, including endometriosis, adenomyosis, interstitial cystitis, abdominal wall pain, Bartholin cyst, mittelschmerz, ectopic pregnancy, and hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing primary from secondary dysmenorrhea, using physical exam maneuvers such as the one-finger test for abdominal wall pain, and recognizing red flags like bilateral shoulder pain indicating hemoperitoneum. The lecture provides actionable guidance on diagnosis and initial management, including the use of oral contraceptives for mittelschmerz and Word catheter or marsupialization for Bartholin cyst abscess.
key_points: Use eight questions for pelvic pain history: location, quality, frequency, duration, aggravating factors, relieving factors, change over time, and radiation.
Secondary dysmenorrhea develops after a period of painless cycles and suggests underlying pathology such as endometriosis or adenomyosis.
Endometriosis diagnosis is confirmed by laparoscopy; physical exam may reveal nodularity in the posterior cul-de-sac.
Adenomyosis can often be diagnosed by history and physical exam (boggy, tender uterus) without imaging in 95% of cases.
Interstitial cystitis is frequently associated with endometriosis and irritable bowel syndrome; consider it when suprapubic pain worsens with bladder filling.
Abdominal wall pain is identified by the one-finger test and Carnett's sign (pain increases with tensing abdominal muscles).
First Bartholin cyst abscess is treated with Word catheter; recurrent abscess requires marsupialization.
Mittelschmerz (mid-cycle ovulation pain) can be managed with oral contraceptives; if persistent, consider continuous OCPs.
In acute pelvic pain, always rule out ectopic pregnancy with a pregnancy test.
Bilateral shoulder pain with inspiration (Kehr's sign) indicates diaphragmatic irritation from intra-abdominal blood, as in ruptured ectopic or hemorrhagic cyst.
